Basic principles of R syntax (applied in the Sources tab)

Pressing ENTER moves the cursor to the next line, it does not command the code to run.

Apply Family: lapply, sapply, tapply

apply란? 행렬, 배열 데이터 구조에서 특정 함수를 반복 적용하게 해주는 함수. for loops & while loops에 비해 빠르고 간편.
apply함수의 기본 로직: apply(X, MARGIN, FUN, ..., simplify=T/F)

X = 입력 데이터. 주로 데이터프레임, 행렬 or 배열
MARGIN = 함수가 적용될 데이터의 차원 (MARGIN=1이면 row 기준, MARGIN=2면 column 기준)
FUN = 적용하고 싶은 특정 함수 (ex. mean, sum, …)
… = FUN에 따른 추가 옵션. 예를 들어 FUN이 mean일 때 결측치를 제거하는 옵션인 na.rm=TRUE를 뒤에 작성할 수 있음.
simplify = 디폴트값은 TRUE, 가능한 경우 결과를 벡터/행렬로 반환. FALSE로 설정하면 결과를 리스트로 반환. (= 즉, 단순화하고 싶은 경우 simplify=T이며, 이는 sapply와 동일한 결과를 반환함)

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
1. What Are Descriptive Statistics?
Descriptive statistics are methods for organizing, summarizing, and presenting observed data.
We usually summarize data in three ways:

Tables
Graphs or figures
Statistic: A rule that reduces data to a single number

Descriptive statistics describe the data we observed.
They do not, by themselves, tell us whether a pattern generalizes to a larger population.

# Example data
scores <- c(72, 81, 76, 88, 91, 84, 77, 95, 82, 84)
scores

 [1] 72 81 76 88 91 84 77 95 82 84


A quick summary can already tell us a great deal about the dataset.

summary(scores)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
     72      78      83      83      87      95

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
2. Variables and Levels of Measurement
Before choosing a statistical summary, we should first ask:

What kind of variable am I working with?


Source: https://www.ijngp.com/post/measurement-scale-noir 
A common classification is:








Level
Main characteristic
Example




Nominal
Categories without order
Gender, media platform


Ordinal
Ordered categories
Satisfaction level


Interval
Equal intervals, no true zero
Temperature in °C


Ratio
Equal intervals and meaningful zero
Age, income, reaction time




In practice, a simpler distinction is often useful:

Categorical variables: represent groups or categories
Quantitative variables: represent numerical amounts


Source: https://www.ijngp.com/post/measurement-scale-noir

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
3. Frequency Distributions

A tabular summary of data showing the frequency (or number) of items in each of several nonoverlapping classes.
The objective is to provide insights about the data that cannot be quickly obtained by looking only at the original data.


Example: Hotel Satisfaction
Suppose 20 guests evaluate a hotel using five response categories.

satis <- c(
  "Below Average", "Average", "Above Average",
  "Above Average", "Above Average", "Above Average",
  "Above Average", "Below Average", "Below Average",
  "Average", "Poor", "Poor",
  "Above Average", "Excellent", "Above Average",
  "Average", "Above Average", "Average",
  "Above Average", "Average"
)

satis <- factor(
  satis,
  levels = c("Poor", "Below Average", "Average",
             "Above Average", "Excellent"),
  ordered = TRUE
)



Frequency Distribution

table(satis)

satis

            2             3             5             9             1 


Using dplyr, we can create a cleaner table.

library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)

  count(rating)

Guidelines for Selecting Number of Classes

Use between 5 and 20 classes.
Data sets with a larger number of elements usually require a larger number of classes.
Smaller data sets usually require fewer classes.


Guidelines for Selecting Width of Classes

Use classes of equal width.

\[
\text{Approximate Class Width}
=
\frac{\text{Largest Data Value} - \text{Smallest Data Value}}
{\text{Number of Classes}}
\]



Relative Frequency Distribution

The relative frequency of a class is the fraction or proportion of the total number of data items belonging to the class.
A relative frequency distribution is a tabular summary of a set of data showing the relative frequency for each class.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
4. Visualizing Categorical Data

Bar Plot

A bar graph is a graphical device for depicting qualitative data.
On the horizontal axis we specify the labels that are used for each of the classes.
A frequency, relative frequency, or percent frequency scale can be used for the vertical axis.
Using a bar of fixed width drawn above each class label, we extend the height appropriately.
The bars are separated to emphasize the fact that each class is a separate category.


barplot(table(hotel$rating))








Using ggplot2, we can create a cleaner plot.
In ggplot2, we build a graph by adding layers with +.

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(hotel)







ggplot(hotel, aes(x=rating))







ggplot(hotel, aes(x=rating)) + 
  geom_bar()







ggplot(hotel, aes(x=rating)) + 
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue")







ggplot(hotel, aes(x=rating)) + 
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue", colour = "black")







ggplot(hotel, aes(x=rating)) + 
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue", colour = "black") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Hotel Ratings",
       x = "Hotel Rating",
       y = "Frequency")







ggplot(hotel, aes(x=rating)) + 
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue", colour = "black") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Hotel Ratings",
       subtitle = "Customer satisfaction ratings from 20 hotel guests",
       x = "Hotel Rating",
       y = "Frequency")







ggplot(hotel, aes(x=rating)) + 
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue", colour = "black") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Hotel Ratings",
       subtitle = "Customer satisfaction ratings from 20 hotel guests",
       x = "Hotel Rating",
       y = "Frequency") +
  theme_classic()










Pie Chart

The pie chart is a commonly used graphical device for presenting relative frequency distributions for qualitative data.
First draw a circle; then use the relative frequencies to subdivide the circle into sectors that correspond to the relative frequency for each class.
Since there are 360 degrees in a circle, a class with a relative frequency of .25 would consume .25(360) = 90 degrees of the circle.


pie(table(hotel$rating))







ggplot(hotel, aes(x = "", fill = rating)) +
  geom_bar(color = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Hotel Ratings",
       fill = "Rating") +
  theme_void()







ggplot(hotel, aes(x = "", fill = rating)) +
  geom_bar(color = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = gsub(" ", "\n", rating)),
    stat = "count",
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
    color = "black",
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 4,
    lineheight = 0.9
  )+
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Hotel Ratings") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
5. Visualizing Quantitative Data

Histogram

Another common graphical presentation of quantitative data is a histogram.
The variable of interest is placed on the horizontal axis.
A rectangle is drawn above each class interval with its height corresponding to the interval’s frequency, relative frequency, or percent frequency.
Unlike a bar graph, a histogram has no natural separation between rectangles of adjacent classes.


st <- as.data.frame(state.x77)
names(st)

[1] "Population" "Income"     "Illiteracy" "Life Exp"   "Murder"    
[6] "HS Grad"    "Frost"      "Area"      

st %>% 
  rename(Life.Exp = "Life Exp") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Life.Exp)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 6,
                 fill = "cornflowerblue",
                 color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Life Expectancy",
       y = "Frequency",
       title = "Distribution of Life Expectancy") +
  theme_minimal()











Bar plot vs. histogram

What is the difference between a bar graph and a histogram?










A bar plot is mainly used for categorical variables.
A histogram is used to display the distribution of a quantitative variable.



Misleading Graphs and Charts: Scale Break









The two graphs display the same data, but the truncated y-axis makes the increase appear much larger.
For bar charts, changing the baseline can substantially change the visual impression of the differences.

When reading a histogram, examine:

center — where most observations are located,
spread — how widely observations vary,
shape — symmetric or skewed,
modality — one peak or several peaks,

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
7. Shape of a Distribution

Symmetry and Skewness
A distribution is symmetric when its left and right sides are approximately balanced.
A distribution is right-skewed when the long tail extends toward larger values.
A distribution is left-skewed when the long tail extends toward smaller values.

set.seed(123)

symmetric_data <- rnorm(1000)
right_skewed_data <- rexp(1000)

tibble(value = symmetric_data) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(title = "Approximately Symmetric Distribution") +
  theme_minimal()









tibble(value = right_skewed_data) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(title = "Right-Skewed Distribution") +
  theme_minimal()










Computing Skewness and Kurtosis in R
The moments package provides convenient functions.

# install.packages("moments")  # Run once if needed
library(moments)

cost <- c(
  91, 78, 93, 57, 75, 52, 99, 80, 97, 62,
  71, 69, 72, 89, 66, 75, 79, 75, 72, 76,
  104, 74, 62, 68, 97, 105, 77, 65, 80, 109,
  85, 97, 88, 68, 83, 68, 71, 69, 67, 74,
  62, 82, 98, 101, 79, 105, 79, 69, 62, 73
)

skewness(cost)

[1] 0.4652214

kurtosis(cost)

[1] 2.344017








ImportantInterpretation caution



Skewness and kurtosis should not be interpreted using a single universal cutoff.
Their practical importance depends on sample size, the statistical model, and the purpose of the analysis.
Visual inspection of the distribution should accompany numerical summaries.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
8. Box Plot, Quartiles, and IQR
A box plot summarizes a quantitative variable using its location and spread.
Important components include:

first quartile: (Q_1)
median: (Q_2)
third quartile: (Q_3)
interquartile range:

[ IQR = Q_3 - Q_1 ]

quantile(cost)

    0%    25%    50%    75%   100% 
 52.00  69.00  75.50  88.75 109.00 

IQR(cost)

[1] 19.75



Box Plot in R

tibble(cost = cost) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = cost)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    y = "Parts Cost",
    title = "Box Plot of Parts Costs"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()










Potential Outliers Using the 1.5 × IQR Rule
A commonly used rule identifies observations outside:
[ Q_1 - 1.5(IQR) ]
and
[ Q_3 + 1.5(IQR) ]
as potential outliers.

q1 <- quantile(cost, 0.25)
q3 <- quantile(cost, 0.75)
iqr <- IQR(cost)

lower_bound <- q1 - 1.5 * iqr
upper_bound <- q3 + 1.5 * iqr

lower_bound

   25% 
39.375 

upper_bound

    75% 
118.375 

cost[cost < lower_bound | cost > upper_bound]

numeric(0)








Warning



An observation flagged by the 1.5 × IQR rule should not automatically be deleted.
It may reflect a data-entry error, a rare but valid observation, or an important feature of the population.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
9. Measures of Central Tendency
The three common measures of central tendency are:

Mean: arithmetic average
Median: middle value after ordering the data
Mode: most frequently observed value


Mean
For a sample,
[ {x} = _{i=1}^{n}x_i ]

mean(cost)

[1] 78.98


The mean uses every observation, so it can be sensitive to extreme values.


Median
The median divides the ordered observations into two halves.

median(cost)

[1] 75.5


The median is less sensitive to extreme observations than the mean.


Mode
Base R does not provide a direct statistical-mode function, but we can obtain it from a frequency table.

get_mode <- function(x) {
  frequency <- table(x)
  names(frequency)[frequency == max(frequency)]
}

get_mode(hotel)

[1] "Above Average"

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
10. Mean and Median Under Skewness
The relationship between the mean and median often provides information about the shape of a distribution.
For a roughly symmetric distribution:
[ Mean Median ]
For a strongly right-skewed distribution, large observations tend to pull the mean upward.

income <- c(30, 32, 35, 36, 38, 40, 41, 42, 45, 150)

mean(income)

[1] 48.9

median(income)

[1] 39


Here, one very large value has a much stronger effect on the mean than on the median.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
11. Measures of Variation
Measures of central tendency tell us where a distribution is located.
Measures of variation tell us how dispersed the observations are.
Common measures include:

Range
Variance
Standard deviation
Interquartile range


Range
[ Range = Maximum - Minimum ]

max(cost) - min(cost)

[1] 57

range(cost)

[1]  52 109




Variance
For a sample,
[ s^2 = ]

var(cost)

[1] 195.7751




Standard Deviation
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance.
[ s = ]

sd(cost)

[1] 13.99197


Because the standard deviation is expressed in the same unit as the original variable, it is usually easier to interpret than variance.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
12. Describing a Dataset in R
R provides several ways to obtain descriptive statistics quickly.

Base R

summary(cost)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  52.00   69.00   75.50   78.98   88.75  109.00

tibble(cost = cost) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(cost),
    median = median(cost),
    sd = sd(cost),
    variance = var(cost),
    min = min(cost),
    max = max(cost),
    iqr = IQR(cost)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 8
      n  mean median    sd variance   min   max   iqr

1    50  79.0   75.5  14.0     196.    52   109  19.8




Grouped Descriptive Statistics
One of the most common tasks in social-science data analysis is to compare descriptive statistics across groups.

set.seed(123)

survey <- tibble(
  condition = rep(c("Control", "Treatment"), each = 50),
  outcome = c(
    rnorm(50, mean = 5.0, sd = 1.2),
    rnorm(50, mean = 5.6, sd = 1.1)
  )
)

survey |>
  group_by(condition) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(outcome),
    sd = sd(outcome),
    median = median(outcome)
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  condition     n  mean    sd median
  <chr>     <int> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
1 Control      50  5.04 1.11    4.91
2 Treatment    50  5.76 0.996   5.77


This type of summary is often the first step before conducting inferential analyses such as a t-test or ANOVA.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
13. The Empirical Rule
For an approximately normal distribution:

about 68% of observations fall within () standard deviation of the mean,
about 95% fall within () standard deviations,
about 99.7% fall within () standard deviations.

Suppose IQ scores have:
[ = 100, = 16 ]
Then approximately 68% of scores are expected to fall between:

mean_iq <- 100
sd_iq <- 16

c(
  lower = mean_iq - sd_iq,
  upper = mean_iq + sd_iq
)

lower upper 
   84   116 


Approximately 95% fall between:

c(
  lower = mean_iq - 2 * sd_iq,
  upper = mean_iq + 2 * sd_iq
)

lower upper 
   68   132 


The 68–95–99.7 rule is an approximation that applies when the distribution is approximately normal.

A good descriptive analysis usually combines numerical summaries and visualization.

The table tells us how much the groups differ.
The plot helps us see how the observations are distributed, including spread, asymmetry, and possible outliers.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Main idea
Do not start by making a graph. Start by asking whether the data are trustworthy and whether each variable means what you think it means.
A useful workflow is:
Question → Audit → Clean → Explore → Reshape → Visualize → Communicate

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Understand what one row means
Before calculating statistics or drawing plots, identify the unit of observation.
Ask:

What does one row represent?
What does one column represent?
Which columns are identifiers or metadata?
Which variables are outcomes, predictors, or descriptive attributes?
Is the dataset already aggregated, or does each row represent an individual event/person/case?

This matters because the same variable can mean different things at different levels of analysis.
For example:

one row = one person;
one row = one survey response;
one row = one social-media post;
one row = one traffic collision;
one row = one country-year.

text:
Variable types

Numeric variables
Numeric variables have values that describe a measurable quantity: how many or how much.

Continuous numeric variable: observations can take values on a continuous scale, such as temperature, income, or distance.
Discrete numeric variable: observations represent counts, such as number of clicks, number of injuries, or number of purchases.



Categorical variables
Categorical variables describe a characteristic or group membership: what type or which category.

Nominal variable: categories have no meaningful ordering, such as borough or vehicle type.
Ordinal variable: categories can be logically ordered, such as satisfaction level or education level.







TipNumbers are not always numeric variables



A variable can be stored as numbers but still be categorical.
For example, if 1 = Seoul, 2 = Busan, and 3 = Incheon, the numbers are codes, not quantities. Computing their mean would not be meaningful.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
What is exploratory data analysis (EDA)?
EDA is the process of learning what a dataset contains before making strong conclusions from it.
EDA usually combines:

Descriptive statistics — numerical summaries of distributions and relationships.
Graphical summaries — visual displays that reveal patterns that a few summary statistics may hide.
Data-quality checks — checks for missing, duplicated, invalid, inconsistent, or unusual values.

EDA and preprocessing are therefore closely connected. We often discover cleaning problems while exploring the data.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
A practical data-audit checklist
Before analysis, ask the following questions.

Rows: How many observations are there?
Columns: How many variables are there?
Variable roles: Which columns are identifiers, attributes, outcomes, or metadata?
Data types: Which variables are numeric, categorical, text, dates, or times?
Ranges: Are minimum and maximum values plausible?
Categories: Are category labels consistent and documented?
Missing values: Where are data missing, and how much is missing?
Duplicates: Are rows or identifiers unexpectedly duplicated?
Invalid values: Are there impossible or undefined codes?
Outliers: Are extreme values errors, or are they valid but rare cases?







TipA useful principle



A preprocessing decision should always answer two questions:

What is wrong or inconvenient about the current value?
Why is the chosen correction appropriate for the analysis?

Never delete or replace observations only because a function makes it easy to do so.

Missingness is one of the most common problems in real project data.

Missing values are not all the same
Suppose borough is missing.
Possible interpretations include:

the collision occurred outside a coded borough;
the location was unavailable;
the field was not entered;

Therefore, this is usually a poor default:

borough_data <- collisions %>%

Outliers: inspect first, decide later
An outlier is an unusual observation. It is not automatically an error.
Possible reasons for an extreme value:

data-entry error;
measurement error;
coding error;
rare but genuine event;
observation from a different population;
unit mismatch.


Summary statistics

collisions %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_injured = mean(injured, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_injured = median(injured, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_injured = sd(injured, na.rm = TRUE),
    q1 = quantile(injured, .25, na.rm = TRUE),
    q3 = quantile(injured, .75, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_injured = max(injured, na.rm = TRUE)

The IQR rule can flag observations for inspection.

q1 <- quantile(collisions$injured, .25, na.rm = TRUE)
q3 <- quantile(collisions$injured, .75, na.rm = TRUE)
iqr_value <- IQR(collisions$injured, na.rm = TRUE)
upper_fence <- q3 + 1.5 * iqr_value

injury_outliers <- collisions %>%
  filter(injured > upper_fence) %>%
  arrange(desc(injured))

injury_outliers %>%
  select(

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Handling missing data: practical options
There is no single correct rule for missing data. Common options include:

Keep missing values
Often the safest default during early EDA.

collisions_clean <- collisions



Filter missing values for a specific analysis
For a borough comparison:

borough_analysis <- collisions_clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(borough))



Create an explicit “Unknown” category
Useful when missingness itself is meaningful for descriptive reporting.

collisions_clean <- collisions_clean %>%
  mutate(
    borough_display = replace_na(borough, "Unknown")
  )



Imputation
Imputation replaces missing values using an estimated value.
Examples include:

mean or median imputation;
group-specific imputation;
regression/model-based imputation;
multiple imputation.

For this introductory class, do not impute automatically. The method must be justified by the variable, the missing-data mechanism, and the purpose of the analysis.

Create useful derived variables
Preprocessing is not only about fixing errors. It also includes creating variables that better represent the analytical question.

Severe collision indicator

    severe_collision = injured > 0 | killed > 0
  )



Time of day

collisions_clean <- collisions_clean %>%
  mutate(
    time_of_day = case_when(
      crash_hour >= 5  & crash_hour < 12 ~ "Morning",
      crash_hour >= 12 & crash_hour < 17 ~ "Afternoon",
      crash_hour >= 17 & crash_hour < 21 ~ "Evening",
      !is.na(crash_hour) ~ "Night",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    time_of_day = factor(
      time_of_day,
      levels = c("Morning", "Afternoon", "Evening", "Night")
